title: Building a Split-Brain Trial
scopeNote: This keeps the trial builder, because the finding is about a procedure as much as about a brain and the learner has to be able to assemble it and take it apart. Cross-cueing, further response channels, chimeric stimuli and the record of conditions switched off one at a time stay in the longer version.
summary: Choose which side of fixation a word appears, how the person is asked to answer, whether the corpus callosum is intact, and how long the word is up. The classic result requires a particular value of all four, and lengthening the exposure alone abolishes it.
learningObjectives: Trace a lateralised stimulus to the hemisphere that receives it.
Explain why the response channel determines whether a trial succeeds.
Explain why a brief presentation is a necessary condition rather than a technical detail.
Explain why split-brain patients are largely unremarkable outside the laboratory.
Distinguish what the procedure shows from the popular claim about two minds.
interactionTypes: four independent controls building a single trial
a schematic redrawn for every combination showing which hemisphere holds the word
an outcome computed from whether the responding hemisphere has the word
a guided build of the classic trial
a second button that removes the one condition the finding depends on
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with all four controls labelled radio groups; each option states its own consequence, so the mapping from side to hemisphere and from response to hemisphere is available without the diagram. The guided buttons move the radios as well as the drawing, so the controls and the figure never disagree. A hemisphere holding the word is shaded and also says so in words inside the box; a cut callosum is drawn broken with a cross and labelled. The diagram carries a description naming the side, the exposure, the callosum, which hemisphere has the word, which one must produce the answer, and whether it can. The outcome tile states the result in words with its reason. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
dataStatus: A schematic. No real patient is described and the diagram is not an anatomy.
simulationNotes: A trial succeeds when the hemisphere that can produce the requested response holds the word. Left of fixation reaches the right hemisphere; speech is produced by the left hemisphere; the left hand is controlled by the right and the right hand by the left. With the callosum intact both hemispheres end up holding the word, and with a long exposure both do as well whatever the callosum is doing, because the eyes can move to it. That last control is the one students never think of and is the reason the finding is about a procedure: ordinary life does not present things for a fraction of a second while the gaze is held still. The caution states that these were a handful of patients with already unusual brains, that surgery was not always complete, that language was not always lateralised in the standard way, and that the popular two-minds reading goes well beyond what the procedure shows.
readmeTopic: the four conditions the classic split-brain result needs, and what happens when one is removed
